'''Ahmet Cemal Eringen'''<ref name="math">{{MathGenealogy|id=147062}}</ref> (February 15, 1921 – December 7, 2009<ref name="SES"/><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.princeton.edu/main/news/bulletin/docs/Bulletin-2010-03-01.pdf |title=Ahmed Eringen, died on December 7, 2009 at the age of 88 (1966-1991, civil engineering and operations research) in Princeton University Bulletin, vol. 99, No: 9, page 2, Obituary section, published March 1, 2010. |access-date=2016-03-31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160701230853/http://www.princeton.edu/main/news/bulletin/docs/Bulletin-2010-03-01.pdf |archive-date=2016-07-01 |url-status=dead }}</ref>) was a Turkish engineering scientist. He was a professor at [[Princeton University]] and the founder of the Society of Engineering Science.<ref name="SOES">[http://ses.egr.uh.edu/honors-awards/ses-fellows ''Ahmed Cemal Eringen'' was elected a fellow of the Society of Engineering Science] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170807233244/http://ses.egr.uh.edu/honors-awards/ses-fellows |date=2017-08-07 }} together with [[L. Stanley Crane#With Conrail|Harold Liebowitz]] and [[Warren Perry Mason]] in 1975.</ref> The [[Eringen Medal]] is named in his honor.<ref name="SOES"/>

== Education ==
Eringen was born in [[Kayseri]], Turkey and studied at the [[Istanbul Technical University]] and graduated with a diploma degree in 1943 and then worked for the Turkish Aircraft Co. until 1944. In 1944–1945, he was a trainee at the [[Glenn L. Martin Company]] and in 1945 was group leader at the Turkish Air League Company. He continued his studies at the [[Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn]] in [[New York City]] where he received his doctorate in [[applied mechanics]] in 1948<ref name="math"/> under the supervision of [[Nicholas J. Hoff]].<ref>''Continuum Mechanics Through the Twentieth Century'', [[Gerard Maugin|Gérard A. Maugin]], 2013</ref>

== Academic life ==
He became assistant professor at the [[Illinois Institute of Technology]] in 1948, associate professor in 1953 and professor in 1955 at [[Purdue University]]. He was appointed as professor of [[aerospace engineering|aerospace]] and [[mechanical engineering]] at [[Princeton University]] in 1966. He became professor of [[continuum mechanics]] in the departments of ''[[Civil Engineering|civil]] and [[geological engineering]]'' and ''the program in [[applied mathematics|applied]] and [[computational mathematics]]''<ref>[http://www.pacm.princeton.edu/ PACM, The Program in Applied & Computational Mathematics at Princeton University.]</ref> at [[Princeton University]]. He retired in 1991 as the dean of the [[Princeton University School of Engineering and Applied Science|School of Engineering and Applied Science]] at [[Princeton University]] and died in 2009.

== Research areas ==
His work deals with [[continuum mechanics]], [[electrodynamics]] of [[continuum mechanics|continua]] and [[Materials science|material theories]].

== Awards ==
In 1981 he received an honorary doctorate from the [[University of Glasgow]] (D.Sc.). In 1973, he received the Distinguished Service Award and the 1976 as named in his honor [[Eringen Medal|A. C. Eringen Medal]] of the Society of Engineering Science, whose president he was in 1963 to 1973.<ref name="SES">{{Cite web |url=http://ses.egr.uh.edu/taxonomy/term/2 |title=A. Cemal Erigen - Society of Engineering Science (SES) |access-date=2024-12-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160325160501/http://ses.egr.uh.edu/taxonomy/term/2 |archive-date=2016-03-25 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Eringen had been married since 1949 and had four children.
